paper_a.title: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis

metadata.description: Paper B (Kasiviswanathan-Lee-Nissim-Raskhodnikova-Smith) extends Paper A (Dwork-McSherry-Nissim-Smith) from foundational central differential privacy with the Laplace mechanism into the realm of private learning theory and the local model. Paper B explicitly cites paper A's epsilon-DP definition and Laplace mechanism as external prior work and builds on them: it introduces private PAC / agnostic learning (using the exponential mechanism, a generalization of Paper A's general-metric mechanism), defines the local privacy model (a per-row variant of Paper A's central indistinguishability), proves equivalence of local learning with the SQ model, and exhibits a separation of the two via the PARITY problem. Both papers are PDF-fallback (math fidelity reduced); confidences are tagged accordingly.

matches.explanation: Paper A's epsilon-Indistinguishability and Paper B's epsilon-Differential Privacy are the standard foundational DP definition: bounded log-ratio of output probabilities for any pair of neighbouring databases. Paper B's node has origin=external with origin_citation pointing directly to Dwork-McSherry-Nissim-Smith [24] (Paper A). Same object up to the rename indistinguishability -> differential privacy that became standard.

Paper A's L_1 sensitivity definition supplies the scale parameter consumed by Paper B's Laplace-mechanism theorem (TP287.1, which cites Dwork et al. [24] and uses GS_f = max |f(z)-f(z')| -- the scalar specialization of L_1 sensitivity). Paper B inlines the global-sensitivity definition into the theorem statement rather than calling it out as a separate node, so the alignment is a definition-vs-definition-inside-theorem match.

Paper A's general-metric sensitivity has no direct counterpart in Paper B; Paper B works only with scalar global sensitivity (used through the Laplace mechanism) and a misclassification-count score function for the exponential mechanism. The general metric formulation is a Paper-A specific contribution.

Paper B uses the Laplace distribution (Lap(...) appears in TP287.1, AP287.4, ASP287.8, LP287.8) but does not factor out the distribution as its own definition node; LP287.8 (sums of Laplace random variables) is the closest analogue but is a concentration lemma, not a distribution definition. We therefore mark Paper A's Lap distribution definition as unmatched at the L1 node-level.

Paper A's appendix-A definitions of (k,epsilon)-simulatability, (k,epsilon)-indistinguishability, and (k,epsilon)-semantic-security (group privacy + Bayesian semantic-security framing) are paper-specific; Paper B does not work with the k-row, simulator, or semantic-security formulations and instead uses the single-neighbor DP definition throughout.

Paper A's Laplace mechanism (proposition PrP286.1 for non-interactive output perturbation, theorem TP286.1 for the adaptive variant, and algorithm AP286.1 'Calibrated Noise') and Paper B's TP287.1 (Laplace Mechanism with Global Sensitivity) state the same foundational result: outputting f(z) + Lap(S(f)/epsilon) is epsilon-DP. Paper B records it as an external citation to Paper A; this is the canonical many-A-to-one-B alignment. Confidence high despite PDF-fallback because the names, types, and the explicit external citation make the identification unambiguous.

Paper A's adaptive interactive Laplace mechanism (AP286.2) handles a sequence of queries with the same noise scale and refusal threshold; Paper B's composition / post-processing claim (ClP287.1) captures the same intuition at a more abstract level (composing k epsilon_i-DP algorithms gives sum-DP). Both formalize sequential private querying; Paper B's claim is the cleaner composition theorem now standard in DP, while Paper A's algorithmic statement predates that framing.

Paper A's general-metric sampling mechanism -- sample y with density proportional to exp(-epsilon * d_M(y, f(x)) / (2 S_M(f))) (theorem TP286.2, algorithm AP286.3, density EP286.1, proof PP286.2) -- is the prototype of what Paper B uses as the 'exponential mechanism': output h with probability proportional to exp(epsilon * q(z,h) / 2). Paper B's LP287.1 acknowledges 'following McSherry-Talwar [44]', the published successor of Paper A's general-metric mechanism. This is the same construction with d_M(y, f(x)) replaced by a score function q(z,h); the privacy proof reduces to the same triangle / sensitivity argument.

Paper A's lower-bound machinery -- the non-interactive 2^Omega(d) lower bound via hybrid arguments, randomized-response separation, the random-subset distribution lemma, the variance bound on the estimator, and the sample-complexity-implies-low-sensitivity lemma -- is a Paper-A specific contribution. Paper B has its own lower bound (TP287.6 separating adaptive vs nonadaptive SQ) but it operates on different objects (SQ queries / MASKED-PARITY), with no node-level correspondence to the Paper-A statistical-distance hybrid argument.

Paper A's worked examples (noisy sum, random-index counter-example, sums and histograms, mean and covariance, distance from a property) are illustrative for the calibrated-noise framework. Paper B does not include analogous worked examples; per Compactness, example nodes do not need 'none' entries, but we record this as a single composite 'none' to make the example-track explicit -- the takeaway is that Paper B has shifted focus from query examples to learning-task examples (PARITY, MASKED-PARITY) at the algorithm level.

Paper A's two remarks (constant-factor optimization in the general-metric density, randomized-response interpretation for {0,1}^d outputs) are minor implementation comments; Paper B has its own remarks (RP287.1, RP287.2) that are unrelated. Per Compactness, remark unmatches do not need 'none' entries -- recorded for completeness but at low confidence.

Paper A's appendix-A equivalence claims (indistinguishability <-> simulatability, indistinguishability <-> semantic security) and their proofs PP286.7 / PP286.8 sit in the foundational-definitions track that Paper B does not revisit; Paper B simply imports the cleaner DP definition. Paper-specific contribution unmatched on the B side.

PAC learning (Valiant) and agnostic learning (Haussler / Kearns-Schapire-Sellie) are external classical learning-theory definitions imported by Paper B with no analogue in Paper A, which predates the private-learning agenda.

Paper B's central definitions of private PAC learning, private agnostic learning, and the corresponding problem statement are the new conceptual contribution that Paper A does not address. They combine Paper A's DP definition with Valiant-style learnability.

Paper B's generic private learner sample-complexity theorem and its VC-dimension corollary are Paper-B-original results: existence of a private agnostic learner with O((ln |H| + ln 1/beta) * max(1/(eps*alpha), 1/alpha^2)) samples. Paper A has no learning-theoretic theorems.
VC dimension (external classical), PARITY, and MASKED-PARITY are concept-class definitions imported or introduced by Paper B for its learning-theoretic results; no counterpart in Paper A.

Paper B's efficient private PAC learner for PARITY (the base learner A, the amplified A^*, their utility/privacy lemmas, and TP287.3) constitute the central construction of Paper B's section 4. They are Paper-B-original and have no analogue in Paper A.

Paper B's local model definitions (local randomizer, LR oracle, local algorithm, local learning, transparent local randomizer) introduce the local DP model. Paper A defines only the central / interactive model and has no local-model counterpart.
Statistical-Query oracle / SQ algorithm / SQ learning (Kearns) are external classical objects imported by Paper B for its local <-> SQ equivalence. Outside Paper A's scope.

Paper B's local <-> SQ simulation track (the local algorithm A_g simulating SQ queries, its accuracy lemma, the local-simulates-SQ theorem, the SQ-simulates-local lemma with rejection sampling, and the equivalence theorem TP287.5 plus separation corollaries) is the structural backbone of Paper B's section 5 and entirely Paper-B-original.

Paper B's MASKED-PARITY adaptive vs nonadaptive SQ separation (algorithm A_MP, its correctness proposition, theorem TP287.6, the Fourier-analytic proof PP287.2 with its proof_step DAG, and the related open problem) is a Paper-B-original separation result with no analogue in Paper A. Note: Paper A's PP286.6 also uses Fourier orthogonality in its variance bound, but the underlying objects differ (statistical-distance hybrid vs SQ-query orthogonality), so we do not claim a node-level match.

Standard concentration inequalities (multiplicative Chernoff, additive Chernoff-Hoeffding, sums of Laplace RVs) collected in Paper B's appendix A. They are textbook tools; not present as nodes in Paper A and unrelated to Paper A's specific contributions.
Paper B's open problem of whether efficient learnability implies efficient private learnability is a Paper-B contribution; Paper A predates the private-learning agenda.

Paper B's remarks on 'anything learnable is privately learnable' and 'learning with noise vs private learning' are commentary on Paper B's own results; no Paper-A counterpart. (Per Compactness, remark unmatches need not be listed; included here for narrative completeness.)
